takeawayReviews.title: Carnival Cruise Lines, Inc. v. Shute (1991)
takeawayReviews.takeaway: Under federal admiralty law, the unnegotiated cruise-ticket forum clause could bind the passengers if reasonable and fundamentally fair. Lack of bargaining alone did not defeat it; the Court did not approve every ticket term or every forum clause.
takeawayReviews.outcome: Individually rewritten after comparison
takeawayReviews.changeReason: Complete Holding identifies the federal admiralty setting and reserves other terms.
takeawayReviews.before: A forum clause printed on a cruise ticket can still bind you even though nobody negotiated it. The test is whether the clause is reasonable and fundamentally fair, not whether you had a say in it.

basis.sourceLocator: tools/r19/data/sections.json :: CTR-027.rule and sections.Holding (effective assembler overlays)
basis.inheritedCitation: 251 Minn. 188, 86 N.W.2d 689 (1957). Supreme Court of Minnesota. Murphy, J. Decided December 20, 1957. The Minnesota Supreme Court held that the store's advertisement for a specifically identified fur stole at a stated price, offered to the first customer to arrive, created an offer that Morris Lefkowitz accepted by satisfying those conditions. The store could not then add an eligibility restriction absent from the advertisement. Lefkowitz, the customer and plaintiff below, was the respondent on appeal and represented himself. Great Minneapolis Surplus Store, Inc., the merchant and defendant below, appealed an order refusing to alter the trial court's findings or grant a new trial. The Supreme Court affirmed, leaving Lefkowitz's $138.50 damages award in place. 251 Minn. at 189-92, 86 N.W.2d at 690-91. The full opinion concerns two newspaper advertisements published a week apart. On April 6, 1956, the store advertised three new fur coats for one dollar each, available at 9 a.m. the following Saturday on a first-come, first-served basis. The advertisement described the coats as worth up to $100. On April 13, the store advertised two pastel mink three-skin scarfs, described as selling for $89.50, and one black lapin stole, described as worth $139.50, for one dollar each. The second advertisement again specified Saturday at 9 a.m. and first-come, first-served availability. The lapin stole was the item that ultimately supported the damages award.

takeawayReviews.takeaway: A valid forum clause does not make otherwise proper venue improper. A clause choosing another federal district is enforced through transfer; one choosing a state or foreign court ordinarily through forum non conveniens. takeawayReviews.title: Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins (1938)
takeawayReviews.takeaway: Federal courts deciding state-law rights ordinarily follow the governing state’s statutes and authoritative court decisions, rather than inventing general federal common law. Erie rejected the contrary Swift approach. It did not decide the railroad’s liability, or eliminate distinct federal rules where the Constitution, Congress or a recognized federal interest supplies them.
takeawayReviews.outcome: Individually rewritten after comparison
takeawayReviews.changeReason: Complete Holding concerns general federal common law; complete Clearfield and Boyle Holdings identify distinct federal-law branches.
takeawayReviews.before: Federal judges hearing a state-law case cannot invent their own version of common law. They must follow the state's law, including what its courts have decided. Here that meant Pennsylvania's rule about a railroad's duty, not a general federal one.

takeawayReviews.title: Ingraham v. Wright (1977)
takeawayReviews.takeaway: The Eighth Amendment’s punishment clause did not govern public-school discipline. The Court found Florida’s common-law limits and judicial remedies adequate process without a prior hearing for this setting. It did not find the alleged beatings reasonable, or decide whether arbitrary, severe punishment could violate substantive due process.
takeawayReviews.outcome: Individually rewritten after comparison
takeawayReviews.changeReason: Complete Holding identifies Florida protections and reserved substantive due-process issue; nonapplication of Eighth Amendment is not approval of paddling severity.
takeawayReviews.before: Paddling a student at school is not cruel and unusual punishment under the Constitution, because that clause covers criminal punishment. Students do have a liberty interest, but state laws limiting paddling and letting parents sue are the process they are owed, so no hearing comes first.

takeawayReviews.takeaway: In 1941, the Court respected the coal agency’s application of “producer” to this arrangement as a reasoned statutory judgment after fair process. takeawayReviews.title: Twin Rivers Paper Co. LLC v. SEC (2019)
takeawayReviews.takeaway: For this direct agency-review petition, standing not apparent from the record needed evidentiary support in the opening brief. Consumer Action’s late submissions failed that requirement. The paper suppliers also fell outside the securities statutes’ zone of interests because their commercial benefit did not align systematically with investor protection.
takeawayReviews.outcome: Individually rewritten after comparison
takeawayReviews.changeReason: Complete Holding conditions opening-brief evidence on standing not otherwise apparent and identifies direct review posture.
takeawayReviews.before: A group that sues on behalf of its members must bring proof of a member's injury with its first brief, not later. Paper suppliers who only happened to benefit from securities rules could not sue either, since the rules were meant for investors.

takeawayReviews.title: Garland v. Cargill (2024)
takeawayReviews.takeaway: The nonmechanical bump stocks at issue did not satisfy the statute’s machinegun definition: each shot required a separate trigger function, and the shooter’s ongoing input prevented automatic firing through one function. This statutory holding did not recognize a constitutional right to bump stocks or classify every rapid-fire accessory.
takeawayReviews.outcome: Individually rewritten after comparison
takeawayReviews.changeReason: Complete Holding includes two separate statutory grounds; old pull-again sentence could falsely imply a fresh finger movement instead of separate mechanical trigger function.
takeawayReviews.before: A bump stock does not turn a rifle into a machine gun. The shooter still has to pull the trigger again for each shot, so the weapon does not fire many shots with one trigger function, and only Congress can change the statute.

takeawayReviews.title: Swiss Federal Supreme Court: contractual penalty decision of September 24, 2024
takeawayReviews.takeaway: In this Swiss decision, a CHF 100,000 contractual penalty was reduced to CHF 10,000 for a minor, nonrecurring breach without demonstrated harm. Commercial experience did not prevent reduction, and lack of damage did not require eliminating the penalty. The comparison is reduction of an excessive penalty, rather than the domestic rule of refusing an unenforceable penalty.
